title: Prayer and a prison (Acts 12)
hook: a man asleep in chains, a house awake all night, and a knock nobody believes
tomorrow: how did a church make a big choice without a vote?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antioch: a name handed to the disciples, and a collection right after. The line: little christs.

The night before a big exam or a hard appointment, sleep can feel impossible. Peter is asleep. King Herod has just killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. Now Peter is in prison, chained between two soldiers, the night before Herod means to bring him out. And he sleeps. Across the city, a house is wide awake. Acts puts it in one line: "Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him."
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `PETER, ASLEEP IN CHAINS.` → `A HOUSE WIDE AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Then a light in the cell. An angel "smote Peter on the side, and raised him up, saying, Arise up quickly. And his chains fell off from his hands." They pass the guards, and the iron gate opens "of his own accord." Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, "where many were gathered together praying." He knocks. A girl named Rhoda knows his voice and is so glad she forgets to open the gate. She runs in to tell them, and the praying people answer: "Thou art mad." "But Peter continued knocking." Christians read that scene two ways. One view: prayer should expect an answer. Jesus said, "all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive." Its best case: it takes him at his word, and keeps prayer from shrinking into a ritual nobody expects to work. Read that way, the house's surprise shows how small their expectation had become. The other view: what matters is that they kept praying, through a night when James was already gone and nothing looked likely, and the answer came anyway, doubt and all. Its best case: it leaves room for honest, frightened people, like the father in Mark's Gospel who cried, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Acts doesn't pick. It tells the story with a straight face and leaves Peter knocking.
screen: `CHAINS FELL OFF.` · `THOU ART MAD.` · `ONE VIEW: PRAY EXPECTING.` · `THE OTHER: KEEP PRAYING THROUGH DOUBT.` · then, large: `PRAYER WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and hold one person going through something long: an illness, a wait, a hard season. Each time your mind wanders, come back to them, the way that house kept coming back all night. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply keep them in mind.
Prayer and a prison. Peter chained between soldiers, and a house praying through the night.
Pocket this one: prayer without ceasing, even in a house that didn't believe the knock. Rest easy.

fork.setup: a friend says the house in Acts 12 shows weak faith: they didn't even believe Rhoda. what's the strongest case for her view?
options: Jesus said ask believing; prayer can expect God to act, not just hope.
doubting people's prayers never get answered, so they got lucky.
prayer is only for calming yourself down, not for asking.
fork.reveal: the 'pray expecting' view rests on Matthew 21:22: whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing. the other view points to Mark 9:24. Acts tells the story and doesn't pick.

chat.says: kayla told me her mom's in the hospital. asked me to pray. i'm scared it won't work. does that count?
options: The house in Acts prayed all night and didn't believe the knock. Scared prayer still counts.
Only if you're certain. Jesus said you'll receive whatever you ask for, believing.
Wait until you feel sure, then pray; doubtful prayers in Acts went unanswered.
chat.meaning: The church prayed without ceasing for Peter, then told Rhoda, Thou art mad. Their prayer was answered, doubt and all.

Herod.meaning: the king who killed James and imprisoned Peter

Rhoda.meaning: a girl in Mary's house who knew Peter's voice

John Mark.meaning: Mary's son, called John, whose surname was Mark

For parents: James is killed with the sword (12:2). The voice names it in one plain clause so the prayer story is not told as a simple success; no detail.
The KJV's 'without ceasing' in Acts 12:5 renders a Greek word others translate 'earnestly' or 'fervently'; the lesson keeps the KJV wording and makes no claim about the Greek. Confirm.

v3 debate: two readings inside the tradition, each with its best case and its own scripture (Matthew 21:22; Mark 9:24). Neither is called right. Confirm both are fairly stated and that the 'small expectation' reading isn't voiced as a scolding.
Herod's death (Acts 12:20–23) is left out for length.
'John Mark' joins the KJV's 'John, whose surname was Mark' (Acts 12:12) into the common short form; the gloss gives the KJV form.
